passage: Joseph, you asked me how to argue without a fight. Here's a story. When I was eleven, my friend Anjali and I disagreed about which team should go first in kabaddi. I shouted, “You're wrong!” and she stormed off. Our teacher took us both aside. She asked me, “Can you say it another way?” I said, “I see it differently. I think we should toss a coin, because that's fair.” Anjali stopped and thought. “I guess that's okay,” she said. I learned that saying “I see it differently, and here's why” is no rejection of the person. We played right after.

qa.q: What game were the friends arguing about?
qa.a: Kabaddi.

qa.q: What did the storyteller feel when Anjali stormed off?
qa.a: The storyteller was probably upset and surprised, since shouting “You're wrong!” had pushed the friend away.

qa.q: What could a child say instead of shouting in a disagreement?
qa.a: A child could say “I see it differently, and here's why,” as the storyteller learned to do.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when she was shouted at compared with when the reason was given?
qa.a: She probably felt attacked when shouted at, and calmer and respected when a reason was offered.

grounding: A child learns to say I see it differently and give a reason, instead of shouting, so disagreement is not rejection of the person.

passage: The bus broke down on the way to the zoo trip, and the teacher went to phone the school. Gopika and Arnab, waiting by the roadside with their class, argued about whether to play word games or sing songs until help arrived. “Songs are boring!” said Arnab loudly. Gopika bit back what she wanted to say. Then she took a breath. “I see it differently. Songs help us all join in, and word games only work for some of us. What do you think?” Arnab folded his arms, then unfolded them. “Okay, maybe one of each,” he said. They started with a song.

qa.q: Where were the children waiting?
qa.a: By the roadside, after the bus broke down.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she bit back what she wanted to say, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at being called boring, but she took a breath and calmly explained her view.

qa.q: What did Gopika say that helped, compared with shouting or sulking?
qa.a: She said “I see it differently,” gave a reason and asked Arnab what he thought.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when Gopika asked what he thought?
qa.a: He probably felt listened to, which may be why he unfolded his arms and offered a compromise.

grounding: A child says I see it differently and gives a reason and asks for the other view, so disagreement is not a rejection of the person.

passage: In the school library in Guwahati, the book club had to choose one book for the term. Jaya slapped a thick fantasy novel on the table. “This one. It's the best book ever written. Anyone who disagrees is wrong.” Lalremsiami felt her face heat. She had wanted the mystery, and part of her wanted to shout, “That's so boring!” Instead she took a breath. “I see it differently. It's six hundred pages, and some of us read slowly. Could we do the mystery now and yours next term?” Jaya frowned, then flipped through the fat book. “Six hundred and twelve,” she admitted. “Okay. Mystery first, then mine.” They shook on it.

qa.q: How many pages did the fantasy novel have?
qa.a: It had six hundred and twelve pages.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when Jaya said anyone who disagrees is wrong?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt annoyed and tempted to shout that the book was boring.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami disagree respectfully?
qa.a: She took a breath, said she saw it differently, gave a reason about the length and slow readers, and offered a fair compromise.

qa.q: What changed Jaya's mind?
qa.a: Jaya checked the page count herself and saw Lalremsiami's point, so she agreed to read the mystery first.

grounding: Shows a child saying I see it differently with a reason instead of shouting, and disagreement not rejecting the person.

passage: “Bruno should sleep inside from now on,” said Kiran. “No way,” said Sachin. “He'll chew the sofa. That's stupid.” Kiran's jaw tightened. “Don't call it stupid.” “Sorry. It's not stupid. I just disagree.” “Why, though?” “Because last time he chewed Papa's chappal and got locked out all day. Outside, he's got his kennel.” Kiran thought. “I see that. But it's winter now, and he shivers at night.” Sachin paused. “Okay, that's fair. What if he sleeps on the veranda with a blanket? Warm, but no sofa.” Kiran grinned. “Deal. I still think inside is nicer, though.” “You're allowed to think that.”

qa.q: What did Bruno chew last time?
qa.a: Bruno chewed Papa's chappal.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when Sachin called the idea stupid?
qa.a: Kiran felt hurt and irritated, jaw tightening at having the idea dismissed.

qa.q: What did Sachin change that kept the talk respectful?
qa.a: Sachin apologised for “stupid”, said he just disagreed, gave his reason and then suggested a middle way.

qa.q: What reason did Kiran give that changed Sachin's mind?
qa.a: Kiran pointed out that it's winter and Bruno shivers at night, which Sachin agreed was fair.

grounding: Shows children learning to say I disagree, and here's why, instead of insulting, so disagreement is not rejection of the person.

passage: I'm Salma. Last year in history, Sumit Sir said the Taj Mahal was built in ten years. I'd read it took more like twenty. My heart was pounding; you don't argue with Sumit Sir. Before, I'd have just sulked. This time I put up my hand. “Sir, I think I see it differently. The book in the library says around twenty years, because the gardens and buildings around it took longer.” The class went silent. Sir looked at me for a long moment, then smiled. “You're right that the whole complex took longer. Good disagreeing, Salma. Bring me that book.” I did. He read from it the next day.

qa.q: How long did the library book say the Taj Mahal took to build?
qa.a: The library book said around twenty years.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling before putting up a hand?
qa.a: Salma felt nervous, heart pounding, because arguing with Sumit Sir felt risky.

qa.q: How did Salma disagree respectfully?
qa.a: Salma said “I think I see it differently” and gave a reason with a source, instead of sulking or accusing Sir of being wrong.

qa.q: How did Sumit Sir respond to being disagreed with?
qa.a: He listened, agreed the whole complex took longer, praised the good disagreeing and asked to see the book.

grounding: Shows a child disagreeing with a teacher by saying I see it differently and giving a reason, instead of sulking.

passage:
Note for Vidya's file, from Gautam (Class 6 teacher), Wednesday

In the group discussion on banning weekend homework, Priyanka said weekends are for rest. Last term Vidya would have shouted "That's rubbish!" and sulked. Today she put up her hand and said, "I see it differently. If there's no weekend homework, Monday gets too heavy. That's why." Priyanka nodded and argued back, and they both kept smiling.

Later Vidya argued that Class 6 should get two extra PE periods. I told her, "I disagree, and here's why: exams are close," and she said, "Okay, but can we have one?" I think the phrase is sticking. I'll put her in charge of the next discussion.

qa.q: What was the group discussion about?
qa.a: Banning weekend homework.

qa.q: How did Priyanka likely feel when Vidya said, "I see it differently"?
qa.a: Respected rather than attacked, which is why she nodded, argued back and kept smiling.

qa.q: What phrase helped Vidya disagree without shouting?
qa.a: "I see it differently… That's why," giving a reason instead of calling the other idea rubbish.

qa.q: How did Gautam model respectful disagreement for Vidya?
qa.a: Gautam said, "I disagree, and here's why: exams are close," showing that disagreeing is about the idea, not the person.

grounding: It is a teacher's note on a child learning to say I see it differently with a reason instead of shouting or sulking.
